title: Print a label for every order, whatever the customer left empty

blocks.text: The warehouse prints one label for every order event it receives. Customers fill in a billing address, a shipping address, both or neither, and the order system passes along `null` for any address that was left empty. Since the label printer was moved to record patterns, some orders come back as "not an order" and others are labelled for the wrong address.

items: a parcel goes to the customer's shipping address, or to the billing address when there is no shipping address on file; use `label(...)` for the line;
a customer with no address at all collects the parcel at the counter: `pickup(...)`;
anything that is not an `Order`, `null` included, is rejected with `IllegalArgumentException`.

blocks.text: The records, `label` and `pickup` are written. About six lines in total.

cases.says: an order whose customer gave one address for both gets a label for that address
a value that is not an order, null included, is rejected with IllegalArgumentException
with two different addresses on file, the label uses the shipping address, not the billing one
an order whose customer has no shipping address is still labelled, for the billing address
an order whose customer has no billing address is labelled for the shipping address
an order whose customer has no address at all gets the pickup label instead of failing

origin.section: A Record Pattern Never Matches null, at Any Depth; var and the Component's Declared Type Do

concepts: A record pattern tests the record's type and binds each component by position; binding names are free, so two components of one type can be bound the wrong way round without a compile error.
A record pattern never matches null at any depth, so a nested record pattern on a component that is null makes the whole pattern fail.
A component pattern that tests nothing (var, or the component's declared type) matches a null component and binds null, so a match does not promise non-null bindings.
